deep.reconstruction:
The page is a table headed 'Indices der Primzahlen im höhern Zahlenreiche', meaning indices (discrete logarithms) in the ring Z[i]. It continues the biquadratic-residue material at the end of the previous page, where the 'Fundamentaltheorem' (biquadratic reciprocity in terms of characters 'Dec.') is stated.

Columns ('Mod.'): the 24 primary Gaussian primes pi of norm 5 to 97, plus the inert prime -3 (norm 9) and -7 (norm 49). The listed moduli are -1±2i, -3, 3±2i, 1±4i, -5±2i, -1±6i, 5±4i, -7, 7±2i, -5±6i, -3±8i, 5±8i, 9±4i. All are primary in Gauss's sense: a+bi ≡ 1 mod 2+2i, i.e. b even and a ≡ 1 or 3 mod 4 according as b ≡ 0 or 2 mod 4.

Second header row ('Basis'): for each pi, a primitive root g modulo pi, so the residue field has order N(pi), of size N-1 for the multiplicative group.

Rows ('Rest'): the unit i, then the primes 1+i, 1-i, and all primary primes of norm up to 193 in order of norm, from -1±2i to -7+12i. The unlabeled last row is -7-12i; I verified this by checking several columns.

Entry: ind_g(x) mod N(pi)-1, defined by g^ind ≡ x (mod pi). An asterisk marks x = pi.

Convention (my inference, verified): in every column ind(i) = (N-1)/4. The values are 1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 7, 7, 9, 9, 10, 10, 12, 13, 13, 15, 15, 18, 18, 22, 22, 24, 24. So each g is chosen with g^{(N-1)/4} ≡ +i, i.e. biquadratic character [g/pi] = i, and not merely a primitive root. Hence ind(x) mod 4 is directly Gauss's biquadratic character: x^{(N-1)/4} ≡ i^{ind x} (mod pi). For -3, g = 1+i would give ind i = 6, while 1-i gives 2; Gauss uses the latter. Consistently, ind(base) = 1 in each column whenever the base is expressible from tabulated entries.

Sample verifications (mine):
- Mod -1+2i: i ≡ 3 (mod 5), g = i = 3. Then 1+i ≡ 4 = 3^2, -3 ≡ 2 = 3^3, -5+2i ≡ 1 = 3^0, all matching.
- Mod -3 (F9): with g = 1-i, g^2 = -2i ≡ i and g^3 ≡ 1+i, so ind i = 2, ind(1+i) = 3, ind(1-i) = 1. Also -1+2i ≡ -(1+i) = g^7 and -1-2i ≡ -(1-i) = g^5.
- Mod 3+2i: i ≡ 5 (mod 13), g = -1-i ≡ 7. Then 7^3 = 5, 7^7 = 6 = 1+i, 7^4 = 9 = 1-i.
- Mod 1+4i: i ≡ 4 (mod 17), g = 1-2i ≡ 10. Then 10^4 = 4, 10^7 = 5, 10^3 = 14.
- Mod -5+2i: i ≡ 17 (mod 29), g = 1+i ≡ 18. Then 18^7 = 17 and 18^22 = 13 = 1-i.
- Mod -7 (F49): (1-2i)^12 ≡ i.
- Base consistency: ind(2-i) = ind(i) + ind(-1-2i) = 10 + 31 ≡ 1 mod 40. Also -1-i gives 30 + 31 ≡ 1 mod 60, and -1-i gives 36 + 37 ≡ 1 mod 72.

Purpose: such a table lets one read off biquadratic (and quadratic) characters of Gaussian primes and test the reciprocity theorem stated on p. 24. Example: Dec((3+2i)/(-1+2i)) = 2 and Dec((-1+2i)/(3+2i)) = 4 ≡ 0, giving a difference of 2. The formula ½(A-1)b + ½(a-1)B + ½Bb gives 2 - 2 + 2 = 2, which agrees.

The archivist's note 'Bd II Nachtrag p. 506, 1876' records that the table was printed in Werke II (2nd ed. 1876).

The left-margin numbers are logarithms belonging to the precession computation on p. 24, e.g. 1536.4751 and 5.6444735. They are not related to the table.
errors: No numerical errors found in the entries spot-checked (columns -1±2i, -3, 3+2i, 3-2i, 1+4i, 1-4i, -5+2i, -7, and the last row).

Header bases as transcribed are partly inconsistent with the entries. Under -3 the entries require g = 1-i, not 1+i. Under 3+2i they require g ≡ -1-i, since -1+i ≡ 4 has order 6 mod 13 and is not a primitive root. Under 1-4i they require g ≡ 1-i ≡ 5 mod 17, since ind(1-i) = 1, whereas 1-2i ≡ 9 is a square. Under 9-4i they require g = 1+4i, since ind(1+4i) = 1 but ind(1+i) = 7. These are most likely transcription misreadings of the overwritten bold base entries rather than Gauss's errors.
The last row lacks its label (it is -7-12i), and its entries for -3±8i and 5-8i are left blank.

results.what: Table of discrete logarithms (indices) in Z[i] modulo all primary Gaussian primes and inert primes of norm ≤ 97, for all Gaussian primes up to norm 193. Primitive roots are normalized so that g^{(N-1)/4} ≡ i, making ind mod 4 equal to the biquadratic character.
results.modern_name: Index (discrete log) tables in Z[i]; quartic residue character tables
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (Werke II, Nachlass, published by Schering 1863/1876); later tables by Jacobi (Canon arithmeticus 1839, rational primes) and Reuschle (1875)

results.what: Use of the table to read biquadratic characters consistent with biquadratic reciprocity (stated on the preceding page)

deep.surprise_reason: The table is a computational aid to Gauss's well-known biquadratic residue theory. The archival note itself shows it was printed in Werke II (Nachlass). The normalization ind(i) = (N-1)/4 is a nice detail but matches his published character convention.

checkable.asserts: Mod -1+2i (i≡3 mod 5, base i): ind(1+i)=2 since 1+i≡4, ind(-3)=3 since -3≡2.
i≡3 mod (-1+2i); the unlabeled bottom row -7-12i ≡ 2 = 3^3, giving index 3 as in the table.
Mod -3: (1-i)^2 = -2i ≡ i, so with base 1-i, ind(i)=2 as tabulated.
Mod 3+2i (i≡5 mod 13), base -1-i≡7 is primitive; ind i=3, ind(1+i)=7, ind(1-i)=4.
-1+i≡4 mod (3+2i) has order 6, so it cannot be the base; the base must be -1-i.
Mod 1+4i (i≡4 mod 17), base 1-2i≡10: ind i=4, ind(1+i)=7, ind(1-i)=3.
Mod 1-4i (i≡13 mod 17), base 1-i≡5: ind i=4, ind(1+i)=5, ind(1-i)=1.
Mod -5+2i (i≡17 mod 29), base 1+i≡18: ind i=7, ind(1-i)=22.
The reciprocity formula of p.24 for A+Bi=3+2i, a+bi=-1+2i gives 2, matching table indices 2 and 4≡0 (mod 4).
